text:
After a conversation with someone new, people tend to underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. Across five studies, Boothby and colleagues found this "liking gap" between strangers in a laboratory, among first-year university students getting to know the people they lived with, and among members of the public at a UK workshop. Coders watching recorded conversations could see how much partners liked each other, yet participants seemed to miss those signals. A larger gap was linked with more negative thoughts about how they themselves had come across.

Why this matters across roles: Conversations can leave people wondering and worrying about what the other person really thought of them. This research suggests those worries may be harsher than how others actually saw them.

One practical takeaway: When someone shares a worry about how a conversation went, we can gently mention that people often judge their own social performance more harshly than their conversation partners do, and invite them to notice any signs of warmth they may have overlooked.

Where the evidence stops:
• Participants were mostly university students, with some community members, in the United States and the UK.
• The studies measured beliefs after conversations and did not test whether learning about the gap changes how people feel or act.
• Among students sharing a residence, the gap was no longer found by the end of the academic year.

Key source: Boothby et al., 2018: https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797618783714
